short: Sloped armour, wide tracks and mass production made it the benchmark tank of 1941.
full:
Approved for production on 19 December 1939 before its prototype was finished, the T-34 left the Kharkov works in September 1940. It combined a 76.2 mm gun, 45 mm armour sloped steeply enough to double its effective thickness, Christie suspension and tracks wide enough to cross mud and snow that immobilised German tanks. About 1,200 were with the Red Army when Germany invaded in June 1941, and their appearance prompted Guderian and others to demand a comparable design.

Early examples were crude: a two-man turret that left the commander loading and aiming, poor optics, and radios in only a fraction of vehicles. The T-34-85 of 1944 fixed the worst of it with an 85 mm gun and a three-man turret. Well over 50,000 were built during the war, more than any other tank of the conflict, and its simplicity mattered as much as its design. Soviet front-line use ended in the mid-1950s, but T-34-85s served other armies from Korea to the Balkans for decades afterwards.
